question: A game studio runs UDP-based game servers on Amazon EC2 instances that players reach directly through Elastic IP addresses; there is no load balancer or CloudFront distribution. After a volumetric attack, the studio wants stronger DDoS detection and mitigation for these servers, real-time attack metrics and round-the-clock access to AWS DDoS experts. Which solution meets these requirements?
choices: Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the EC2 instances and add a rate-based rule for UDP floods
Rely on AWS Shield Standard, which applies to every resource in the account automatically
Enable Amazon GuardDuty and have the security team respond manually to the findings it raises
Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced and add the Elastic IP addresses as protected resources
explanation: Shield Advanced can protect Elastic IP addresses and the EC2 instances associated with them against network and transport layer attacks. It adds real-time attack metrics and access to the Shield Response Team, which needs a Business or Enterprise Support plan.

choiceExplanations.0: AWS WAF inspects HTTP(S) requests for resources such as CloudFront distributions and Application Load Balancers; it cannot be attached to EC2 instances or Elastic IP addresses that carry UDP game traffic.
choiceExplanations.1: Shield Standard protects every AWS customer automatically, but it does not add the real-time attack metrics or the access to the Shield Response Team that Shield Advanced provides.
choiceExplanations.2: Amazon GuardDuty is a threat detection service that generates findings; it is not a DDoS mitigation service and gives no access to the Shield Response Team.

resources.title: List of AWS resources that AWS Shield Advanced protects
AWS Shield Advanced capabilities and options

question: An online retailer protects the Application Load Balancer in front of its checkout API with AWS Shield Advanced and has a Business Support plan. During a suspected attack the operations team does not want to open a case and wait: the Shield Response Team should contact the on-call engineer directly when the API becomes unhealthy. What should the team configure?
choices: Enable Shield Advanced proactive engagement, with a Route 53 health check on the ALB protection and a contact
Add the load balancer and the CloudFront distribution in front of it to a Shield Advanced protection group
Rely on Shield Advanced cost protection and request service credits from AWS Support after the attack
Keep AWS Shield Standard on the load balancer and add a CloudWatch alarm that pages the on-call engineer
explanation: With proactive engagement, the Shield Response Team contacts the people you list when the Route 53 health check associated with a protected resource becomes unhealthy during an event that Shield Advanced detects. It needs a Business or Enterprise Support plan, an associated health check and at least one contact.

choiceExplanations.1: Protection groups combine protected resources so detection and mitigation treat them as one unit; they do not make the Shield Response Team contact anyone.
choiceExplanations.2: Cost protection provides service credits for bill spikes after an attack; it does not make the Shield Response Team reach out during the event.
choiceExplanations.3: Shield Standard is applied automatically and does not include Shield Response Team support, and a CloudWatch alarm would only notify your own staff.

resources.title: Setting up proactive engagement for the SRT to contact you directly
Health-based detection using health checks with Shield Advanced and Route 53

question: EC2 workloads and container images in Amazon ECR must be scanned for known software vulnerabilities. The security team wants resources rescanned automatically when a new CVE affecting them is published, with nobody scheduling scan runs. Which service should it use?
choices: Amazon GuardDuty
Amazon Macie
Amazon Inspector
AWS Config
explanation: Amazon Inspector automatically discovers EC2 instances, ECR container images and Lambda functions and continually scans them for software vulnerabilities. It rescans resources when a new CVE that affects them is published, so nobody has to schedule scans.

choiceExplanations.0: Amazon GuardDuty is a threat detection service that analyzes logs and other data sources for suspicious activity; it does not scan workloads for software vulnerabilities.
choiceExplanations.1: Amazon Macie discovers sensitive data in Amazon S3, so it does not scan compute workloads or container images for vulnerabilities.
choiceExplanations.3: AWS Config records resource configurations and evaluates them against rules; it does not scan software for known vulnerabilities.

resources.title: Automated scan types in Amazon Inspector

question: Amazon Inspector is producing many findings with high base CVSS scores. The security team wants severity values that reflect its own environment, for example whether an affected EC2 instance actually has an open network path from the internet. Which Amazon Inspector capability provides this?
choices: The Amazon Inspector risk score
Amazon Inspector suppression rules
Amazon Inspector findings reports in CSV format
The Amazon Inspector delegated administrator account
explanation: Amazon Inspector adjusts the base score of a vulnerability to your compute environment. For example, it can lower the score for an instance that has no open network path to the internet, which helps you prioritize remediation.

choiceExplanations.1: Suppression rules hide findings that match a filter from your views; they do not recalculate severity.
choiceExplanations.2: Findings reports export findings in CSV or JSON format; they do not change how severity is scored.
choiceExplanations.3: A delegated administrator lets one account manage Amazon Inspector for the organization; it does not change finding scores.

question: A widely used library is reported to contain a critical vulnerability. A company with 60 accounts in AWS Organizations must quickly find which of its EC2 instances, Amazon ECR container images and AWS Lambda functions are affected, review the results from a single account, and avoid running or scheduling scans itself. Which solution should it use?
choices: Amazon GuardDuty, enabled for the organization with a delegated administrator account
Amazon Inspector, activated for the organization from a delegated administrator account
AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager, using a patch policy that covers all of the accounts
Amazon Detective, with a behavior graph that includes all of the member accounts
explanation: Amazon Inspector scans EC2 instances, ECR images and Lambda functions for software vulnerabilities and rescans when a new CVE is published, so no scans are launched manually. A delegated administrator can activate it for the whole organization and see aggregated findings from every member account.

choiceExplanations.0: Amazon GuardDuty detects threats such as suspicious activity found in logs; it does not report vulnerable software packages in instances, images or functions.
choiceExplanations.2: Patch Manager applies patches to managed nodes such as EC2 instances; it does not scan ECR images or Lambda functions for vulnerable packages.
choiceExplanations.3: Amazon Detective helps analyze and investigate the root cause of security findings and suspicious activity; it does not scan workloads for software vulnerabilities.

resources.title: Automated scan types in Amazon Inspector

question: A few EBS-backed EC2 instances run a supported Linux image on which the SSM Agent cannot be installed, so Amazon Inspector is not scanning them. The company still needs operating system package vulnerability findings for them without installing anything. What should it do?
choices: Keep the Amazon Inspector scan mode on agent-based scanning and let it discover the unmanaged instances
Create an Amazon Inspector suppression rule that matches the instances that have no SSM Agent installed
Turn on GuardDuty Malware Protection for EC2 so that it reports the vulnerable operating system packages
Set the Amazon Inspector EC2 scan mode to hybrid, which scans instances without the agent from EBS snapshots
explanation: In hybrid scan mode, Amazon Inspector uses the agent-based method for instances managed by Systems Manager and an agentless method for eligible EBS-backed instances that are not SSM managed. The agentless method collects the software inventory from EBS snapshots.

choiceExplanations.0: Agent-based scan mode scans only the instances that Systems Manager manages, so the unmanaged instances would stay unscanned.
choiceExplanations.1: Suppression rules hide matching findings from your views; they do not make Amazon Inspector scan more instances.
choiceExplanations.2: GuardDuty Malware Protection for EC2 scans EBS volumes for malware; it does not produce vulnerability findings for operating system packages.

resources.title: Scanning Amazon EC2 instances with Amazon Inspector

question: Customer exports sit in many Amazon S3 buckets. The security team wants an automatic inventory of which buckets are public, unencrypted or shared with other accounts, and it also needs to locate personal data inside the objects, without deploying agents. Which service should it use?
choices: Amazon GuardDuty
AWS Config
Amazon Inspector
Amazon Macie
explanation: Amazon Macie keeps an inventory of S3 general purpose buckets and evaluates their security and access control, including public access, encryption and sharing. It also discovers sensitive data such as personal information inside the objects.

choiceExplanations.0: GuardDuty S3 Protection watches S3 data events for suspicious access; it does not classify the personal data inside the objects.
choiceExplanations.1: AWS Config records configurations and evaluates them against rules, but it does not analyze object contents to find personal data.
choiceExplanations.2: Amazon Inspector scans EC2 instances, container images and Lambda functions for software vulnerabilities, not S3 data.

question: Employee IDs in a company's systems follow the pattern EMP followed by seven digits. The security team wants Amazon Macie to find these IDs in S3 objects, but the detection criteria that Macie provides do not cover this format. Which Macie feature should it use?
choices: Macie managed data identifiers
Macie custom data identifiers
Macie allow lists
Macie finding suppression rules
explanation: A custom data identifier is a set of criteria that you define, based on a regular expression and optional keywords, to detect sensitive or proprietary data such as employee IDs that the managed data identifiers do not cover.

choiceExplanations.0: Managed data identifiers are the built-in detection criteria that Macie provides for common sensitive data types, so a company-specific pattern needs a custom identifier.
choiceExplanations.2: Allow lists define text and patterns that Macie should ignore, such as public phone numbers or test data; they do not add detection criteria.
choiceExplanations.3: Suppressing findings hides them from the findings list; it does not add detection criteria.

question: A health analytics firm keeps CSV, JSON, PDF and Word exports in S3 buckets across 60 accounts in AWS Organizations. Compliance must locate objects that contain personal health information, review all results from one central account and receive EventBridge notifications, with the LEAST operational overhead and no custom code. Which solution meets these requirements?
choices: Amazon Macie, with an administrator account designated through AWS Organizations
Amazon GuardDuty with S3 Protection, managed from a delegated administrator account
Amazon Comprehend PII detection jobs that the team starts for the buckets in each account
Amazon Detective, with a behavior graph that includes all of the member accounts
explanation: Macie discovers sensitive data in S3 objects with machine learning and pattern matching, supports formats such as CSV, JSON, PDF and Word, and lets a designated administrator manage member accounts through AWS Organizations. It also publishes findings to Amazon EventBridge, with no custom code.

choiceExplanations.1: GuardDuty S3 Protection monitors S3 data events for suspicious access; it does not find personal health information inside the objects.
choiceExplanations.2: Amazon Comprehend can detect PII entities in text documents through jobs that you create, run and collect results from yourself; it does not give Macie's bucket inventory, findings and organization-wide administration.
choiceExplanations.3: Amazon Detective is used to investigate the root cause of findings and suspicious activity; it does not scan S3 objects for sensitive data.

resources.title: Managing multiple Macie accounts as an organization

question: The Macie administrator of a company with 80 member accounts wants Macie to keep evaluating all S3 buckets in the organization and analyze a sample of representative objects, giving broad visibility into where sensitive data probably resides, without anyone defining jobs or choosing buckets. The team will run deeper analyses on the riskiest buckets later. What should the administrator use?
choices: A one-time Macie sensitive data discovery job that analyzes every object in all of the buckets
Macie custom data identifiers that are enabled for every member account in the organization
Macie automated sensitive data discovery, enabled by the Macie administrator for the organization
Macie policy findings, which report the security settings of every bucket in the organization
explanation: Automated sensitive data discovery continually evaluates the S3 bucket inventory and uses sampling to select and analyze representative objects, giving broad visibility. It covers all general purpose buckets, including those of member accounts, unless the administrator excludes some, and jobs can follow for deeper analysis.

choiceExplanations.0: A discovery job is defined and run by you for chosen buckets, once or on a schedule; it is the deeper, targeted option rather than continual sampling that needs no definitions.
choiceExplanations.1: Custom data identifiers define what to look for; they do not decide which buckets or objects are analyzed.
choiceExplanations.3: Policy findings report potential issues with bucket security and access control, such as public access; they do not analyze object contents for sensitive data.

question: To reduce the load on its EC2 web servers that terminate HTTPS, a company wants to offload SSL/TLS processing and keep the servers' private keys inside single-tenant hardware that only the company controls. Which AWS service should it use?
choices: AWS CloudHSM
AWS KMS
AWS Certificate Manager
AWS Secrets Manager
explanation: AWS CloudHSM provides single-tenant hardware security modules that you control. Web servers can offload part of the SSL/TLS computation to a CloudHSM cluster, which also stores the servers' private keys in the HSMs.

choiceExplanations.1: AWS KMS protects keys in HSMs that the KMS service operates for all customers, so it does not give the company its own single-tenant HSMs for web server private keys or SSL/TLS offload.
choiceExplanations.2: AWS Certificate Manager creates, stores and renews SSL/TLS certificates, but it is not a single-tenant HSM that the company controls.
choiceExplanations.3: AWS Secrets Manager manages and rotates secrets such as database credentials; it is not an HSM and does not offload SSL/TLS processing.

resources.title: Improve your web server security with SSL/TLS offload in AWS CloudHSM

question: Amazon EBS and Amazon S3 must encrypt data with AWS KMS keys whose key material is generated and stored in single-tenant hardware security modules that the company owns in its own AWS account. Which KMS option meets this requirement?
choices: A KMS external key store backed by a key manager outside AWS
A KMS key with imported key material from an on-premises HSM
A KMS multi-Region key replicated to a second Region
A KMS custom key store backed by a CloudHSM cluster in the account
explanation: A KMS custom key store backed by an AWS CloudHSM cluster generates and stores the key material of KMS keys in HSMs that you own and manage. The KMS keys can still be used with AWS services that support customer managed keys.

choiceExplanations.0: An external key store keeps key material in a key manager outside AWS, not in HSMs that run in the company's own AWS account.
choiceExplanations.1: Imported key material is protected in the standard AWS KMS key store, which is not a single-tenant HSM that the company owns.
choiceExplanations.2: Multi-Region keys are standard KMS keys replicated across Regions, and they are not supported in custom key stores, so they are not backed by the company's own HSMs.

question: A bank's document-signing service uses a PKCS #11 library with RSA private keys. The keys must stay in single-tenant, FIPS-validated hardware, and the signing service must keep working if one Availability Zone fails. Which solution meets these requirements?
choices: AWS KMS asymmetric RSA keys in the standard key store, with a multi-Region replica in a second Region
An AWS CloudHSM cluster that contains two HSMs, both of them placed in the same Availability Zone
An AWS CloudHSM cluster with HSMs in two Availability Zones, accessed through the PKCS #11 library
A KMS custom key store backed by a CloudHSM cluster that has HSMs in two Availability Zones
explanation: CloudHSM clusters use single-tenant HSMs, support the PKCS #11 library and keep every HSM in the cluster synchronized. Placing the HSMs in more than one Availability Zone keeps the cluster available if one zone fails.

choiceExplanations.0: The AWS KMS standard key store uses a shared fleet of HSMs rather than single-tenant ones, and applications call the KMS API instead of a PKCS #11 library.
choiceExplanations.1: Both HSMs sit in one Availability Zone, so an outage of that zone takes the whole cluster down; spreading HSMs across zones provides the redundancy.
choiceExplanations.3: Custom key stores support symmetric encryption KMS keys only, so they cannot hold RSA signing keys, and applications use the KMS API rather than PKCS #11.

question: Applications use keys stored in an AWS CloudHSM cluster through the PKCS #11 library. The security team must control which staff can manage the HSM users and which can create and use keys, and AWS must not be able to view or change these permissions. How should the team set this up?
choices: Write IAM policies that allow selected engineers to create and use keys on the CloudHSM cluster
Create CloudHSM users on the HSMs: admins who manage users and crypto users who manage and use keys
List the engineers as key users in a KMS key policy that covers the keys stored on the cluster
Limit the security group of the cluster's HSMs to the IP addresses of the selected engineers' workstations
explanation: CloudHSM has its own HSM users, separate from IAM users. An admin can manage users, and a crypto user can create, delete, share, import and export keys and use them for cryptographic operations. AWS cannot view or modify the users or keys.

choiceExplanations.0: IAM controls API actions such as creating HSMs; once an HSM exists you authenticate to it with HSM user credentials, which are distinct from IAM users.
choiceExplanations.2: A KMS key policy governs KMS keys, and keys that applications use directly through PKCS #11 are not KMS keys; they are managed by HSM users on the cluster.
choiceExplanations.3: A security group only controls network access to the HSMs; it does not separate who may manage users from who may create and use keys.

resources.title: HSM user types for CloudHSM CLI

question: Windows workloads are moving to AWS, including Amazon RDS for SQL Server with Windows authentication and SharePoint servers on EC2. The company needs an actual Microsoft Active Directory that AWS hosts and manages, with Group Policy support and no domain controllers to patch. Which service meets these needs?
choices: AD Connector
AWS Managed Microsoft AD
Amazon Cognito user pools
AWS IAM Identity Center
explanation: AWS Managed Microsoft AD is powered by an actual Windows Server Active Directory that AWS manages. It works with SharePoint and SQL Server workloads and lets you administer Group Policy with familiar Active Directory tools.

choiceExplanations.0: AD Connector is a proxy to an existing on-premises directory, it is not compatible with RDS for SQL Server, and it does not host a directory in AWS.
choiceExplanations.2: Amazon Cognito user pools are a user directory for web and mobile applications; they do not provide an Active Directory domain for Windows workloads.
choiceExplanations.3: AWS IAM Identity Center connects workforce users to AWS accounts and applications and can use a directory as its identity source, but it does not provide an Active Directory with Group Policy.

question: AWS Managed Microsoft AD runs in a shared services account. Teams in 20 other accounts of the same AWS Organization want to join their EC2 instances to this domain without creating a separate directory in every account. Which Directory Service feature should they use?
choices: AWS Managed Microsoft AD directory sharing
AWS Managed Microsoft AD multi-Region replication
AWS Managed Microsoft AD schema extensions
AD Connector seamless domain join
explanation: Directory sharing lets you share one AWS Managed Microsoft AD with other AWS accounts, inside or outside the organization, so EC2 instances there can join the domain seamlessly without a directory in each account.

choiceExplanations.1: Multi-Region replication copies the directory data to other AWS Regions; it is not a way to share a directory across accounts.
choiceExplanations.2: Schema extensions let you extend the directory schema; they do not make the directory available to other accounts.
choiceExplanations.3: AD Connector forwards requests to an on-premises directory and can join instances to that on-premises domain; it does not share an AWS Managed Microsoft AD.

resources.title: Share your AWS Managed Microsoft AD

question: A manufacturer keeps 4,000 users in an on-premises Active Directory. It is moving Windows applications, including SharePoint and SQL Server Always On, to EC2. The applications need domain controllers in AWS with Group Policy and schema extensions, users must keep being managed on premises, and the company wants the LEAST operational overhead. Which solution should the company use?
choices: AD Connector, connected to the on-premises directory over AWS Direct Connect
An Amazon Cognito user pool federated with the on-premises directory through SAML
Self-managed Windows Server domain controllers on EC2, added to the on-premises forest
AWS Managed Microsoft AD, with a trust relationship to the on-premises directory
explanation: AWS Managed Microsoft AD is a real Active Directory run by AWS that works with SharePoint and SQL Server Always On, supports schema extensions and Group Policy, and can trust the on-premises directory so users stay managed there. AWS handles monitoring, snapshots and recovery.

choiceExplanations.0: AD Connector is a proxy that forwards sign-in requests to the on-premises directory; it does not provide domain controllers in AWS.
choiceExplanations.1: Amazon Cognito user pools authenticate application users; they do not provide domain controllers, Group Policy or schema extensions for Windows server workloads.
choiceExplanations.2: Domain controllers on EC2 can work, but the company must patch, back up and monitor them itself, which is more operational overhead than a managed directory.

resources.title: Connect AWS Managed Microsoft AD to your existing Active Directory infrastructure

question: Amazon WorkSpaces is registered with AWS Managed Microsoft AD. Employees have accounts only in the company's on-premises Active Directory and must sign in to their WorkSpaces with those credentials. Which configuration between the two directories is required?
choices: A one-way trust in which AWS Managed Microsoft AD trusts the on-premises directory
A one-way trust in which the on-premises directory trusts AWS Managed Microsoft AD
A two-way trust between AWS Managed Microsoft AD and the on-premises directory
DNS conditional forwarders only, pointing the on-premises DNS servers at the AWS directory
explanation: A two-way trust is required for AWS applications such as Amazon WorkSpaces, so that AWS Managed Microsoft AD can query the users and groups in the self-managed directory. A one-way trust is enough for EC2, RDS and FSx but not for these applications.

choiceExplanations.0: One-way trusts work for EC2, RDS and FSx, but AWS applications such as WorkSpaces need a two-way trust so that AWS Managed Microsoft AD can query the on-premises users and groups.
choiceExplanations.1: A one-way trust is not enough for AWS applications such as WorkSpaces, which require a two-way trust so that AWS Managed Microsoft AD can query the users and groups in the on-premises directory.
choiceExplanations.3: DNS conditional forwarders are a prerequisite for creating a trust, but without the trust itself the on-premises users cannot authenticate.

resources.title: Creating a trust relationship between your AWS Managed Microsoft AD and self-managed AD

question: Dozens of accounts in AWS Organizations need a baseline security group, which allows management access only from the corporate network, attached to EC2 instances in all current and future accounts and managed centrally from one place. Which service should be used?
choices: AWS Organizations service control policies
Amazon GuardDuty
AWS Firewall Manager
AWS Network Firewall
explanation: Firewall Manager security group policies apply common security groups to the accounts and resources you specify across an organization, and they also apply to new in-scope accounts and resources.

choiceExplanations.0: Service control policies set the maximum permissions for IAM users and roles; they do not create or attach security groups.
choiceExplanations.1: Amazon GuardDuty is a threat detection service that analyzes logs and other data sources; it does not manage security groups.
choiceExplanations.3: AWS Network Firewall filters traffic at the perimeter of a VPC; it does not attach security groups to instances.

resources.title: Using security group policies in Firewall Manager to manage Amazon VPC security groups

question: AWS Firewall Manager is in use across an organization, and the team wants AWS Network Firewall protection deployed automatically to the VPCs of the in-scope accounts, including VPCs created later. Which Firewall Manager policy type should it create?
choices: A Firewall Manager AWS WAF policy
A Firewall Manager Network Firewall policy
A Firewall Manager Shield Advanced policy
A Firewall Manager security group policy
explanation: A Firewall Manager Network Firewall policy applies AWS Network Firewall protection to the VPCs of the organization. Firewall Manager automatically adds protection to resources that are added to in-scope accounts.

choiceExplanations.0: A WAF policy deploys web ACL rule groups to web application resources such as load balancers and CloudFront distributions, not Network Firewall to VPCs.
choiceExplanations.2: A Shield Advanced policy applies Shield Advanced protections to the resource types you specify; it does not deploy Network Firewall.
choiceExplanations.3: A security group policy manages Amazon VPC security groups; it does not deploy Network Firewall.

question: A platform team must block DNS queries for domains on a company-maintained deny list in every VPC across 120 accounts in AWS Organizations, including VPCs created in the future, with the LEAST operational overhead. Which solution meets these requirements?
choices: Define the rule groups in the Firewall Manager administrator account and enforce them with a Firewall Manager DNS Firewall policy
Share DNS Firewall rule groups with the other accounts through AWS RAM and let each account owner associate them with its VPCs
Deploy AWS Network Firewall in every VPC and add a stateful domain-list rule group that contains the denied domains
Attach an AWS Organizations service control policy to the organization root that denies DNS queries to the listed domains
explanation: A Firewall Manager DNS Firewall policy associates the DNS Firewall rule groups defined in the administrator account with the VPCs in scope across the organization, and it keeps doing so as accounts and resources are added.

choiceExplanations.1: Sharing the rule groups through AWS RAM makes them usable in other accounts, but each account owner must still associate them with every VPC, including new ones.
choiceExplanations.2: AWS Network Firewall has no visibility into queries made through the Route 53 Resolver, so it cannot filter these DNS queries.
choiceExplanations.3: Service control policies limit the actions IAM principals can perform; they do not filter DNS queries.

resources.title: Using Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall policies in Firewall Manager

question: An AWS Organizations organization with all features enabled is adopting AWS Firewall Manager to enforce security group policies in its member accounts. Which TWO steps are required before Firewall Manager can create and monitor these policies? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Designate an AWS Firewall Manager default administrator account for the organization
Enable Amazon GuardDuty in every member account and in every Region
Enable AWS Security Hub in every member account of the organization
Enable AWS Config in the member accounts and in the Regions that hold the resources to protect
Create an organization trail in AWS CloudTrail for all of the accounts
explanation: Firewall Manager needs a default administrator account for the organization, and AWS Config must be enabled in the member accounts and Regions that contain the resources to protect so that Firewall Manager can monitor policy compliance.

choiceExplanations.1: Amazon GuardDuty is a threat detection service and is not among the Firewall Manager prerequisites.
choiceExplanations.2: Firewall Manager can send findings to Security Hub CSPM, but enabling Security Hub is not among the Firewall Manager prerequisites.
choiceExplanations.4: An organization trail records API activity; it is not among the Firewall Manager prerequisites.

resources.title: Enabling AWS Config for using Firewall Manager

question: Continuous automated checks against standards such as the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark and PCI DSS are needed for all of a company's AWS accounts, with a security score and a single list of failed controls, without writing the checks itself. Which service should the security team use?
choices: Amazon GuardDuty
Amazon Detective
Amazon Inspector
AWS Security Hub CSPM
explanation: AWS Security Hub CSPM runs continuous automated checks against security standards such as AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, CIS and PCI DSS. It uses the results to calculate security scores and to show the accounts and resources that need attention.

choiceExplanations.0: Amazon GuardDuty detects threats by analyzing logs and other data sources; it does not run checks against security standards.
choiceExplanations.1: Amazon Detective helps investigate the root cause of findings and suspicious activity; it does not check accounts against security standards.
choiceExplanations.2: Amazon Inspector scans EC2 instances, container images and Lambda functions for vulnerabilities and network exposure; it does not check accounts against security standards.

resources.title: Introduction to AWS Security Hub CSPM

question: Workloads run in four AWS Regions, each with AWS Security Hub CSPM enabled. The security team wants to review and update the findings from all four Regions from a single Region. Which Security Hub CSPM feature should it configure?
choices: Security Hub CSPM cross-Region aggregation
Security Hub CSPM automation rules
Security Hub CSPM custom insights
Security Hub CSPM security standards
explanation: With cross-Region aggregation you choose a home Region and linked Regions. Findings, finding updates, insights, control compliance statuses and security scores from the linked Regions are replicated to the home Region, and updates made there are reflected in the linked Regions.

choiceExplanations.1: Automation rules update or suppress findings that match criteria, and a rule applies only in the Region where it is created; they do not bring findings together from other Regions.
choiceExplanations.2: An insight is a collection of related findings defined by a filter or aggregation; it does not collect findings from other Regions.
choiceExplanations.3: Security standards are sets of controls that Security Hub CSPM checks; they do not consolidate findings from several Regions.

resources.title: Understanding cross-Region aggregation in Security Hub CSPM

question: An in-house vulnerability scanner writes its results as JSON files. The security team wants those results shown next to the findings from Amazon GuardDuty and Amazon Inspector, in a common format, so that a Lambda function can react to critical ones. What should the team do?
choices: Add the scanner's output to Amazon Detective as an additional data source
Upload the scanner's results to Amazon GuardDuty as a custom threat list
Import the scanner's results into AWS Security Hub CSPM in the AWS Security Finding Format
Load the scanner's results into Amazon Inspector as additional vulnerability findings
explanation: Security Hub CSPM can consume findings from custom products through the BatchImportFindings operation when they use the AWS Security Finding Format. The findings then appear with those from GuardDuty and Inspector, and EventBridge rules can invoke a Lambda function for specific findings.

choiceExplanations.0: Amazon Detective builds behavior graphs from log data to help investigate the root cause of findings; it is not a place to import findings from other scanners.
choiceExplanations.1: A GuardDuty threat list holds known malicious IP addresses that GuardDuty uses to generate findings; it does not carry vulnerability scan results.
choiceExplanations.3: Amazon Inspector creates findings from its own scans of EC2 instances, container images and Lambda functions; it is not a place to import results from other scanners.

resources.title: Integrating Security Hub CSPM with custom products
Introduction to AWS Security Hub CSPM

question: A security operations team uses AWS Security Hub CSPM across its organization. Findings from production accounts must be raised to CRITICAL severity automatically, without running any code, and every critical finding must create a ticket in the team's external ticketing system. Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Enable cross-Region aggregation in Security Hub CSPM with a home Region
Create a Security Hub CSPM automation rule that raises matching findings to CRITICAL
Create a Security Hub CSPM custom insight that filters on critical findings
Enable the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard in each account
Create an EventBridge rule for critical Security Hub CSPM findings that targets the ticketing system
explanation: Automation rules update findings, for example raising their severity, as Security Hub CSPM ingests them and need no code. Security Hub CSPM also sends findings to Amazon EventBridge, whose rules can send specific findings to third-party tools such as a ticketing system.

choiceExplanations.0: Cross-Region aggregation brings findings from linked Regions into a home Region; it does not change severity or create tickets.
choiceExplanations.2: A custom insight groups and filters findings for review; it does not change severity or create tickets.
choiceExplanations.3: A security standard adds security checks that produce control findings; it does not raise severity automatically or create tickets.

resources.title: Automatically modifying and acting on findings in Security Hub CSPM
Understanding automation rules in Security Hub CSPM

question:
GuardDuty reports unusual API calls made with an EC2 instance's role. A security analyst must see, in interactive visualizations, how that role's activity and the instance's network traffic changed over the past weeks, without building log pipelines or writing queries.
Which service should the analyst use?
choices: Amazon GuardDuty
AWS Security Hub CSPM
Amazon Detective
Amazon Inspector
explanation: Amazon Detective automatically collects log data such as AWS CloudTrail logs, VPC flow logs and GuardDuty findings, and uses it to build interactive visualizations of an entity's activity over time. Analysts can investigate a finding without collecting or querying logs themselves.

choiceExplanations.0: Amazon GuardDuty is the threat detection service that produces the finding in the first place. Looking back at what the role and instance did before and after the finding is what Detective adds.
choiceExplanations.1: AWS Security Hub CSPM collects security findings and runs security-standard checks to give one view of the security state. It does not build visualizations of an entity's activity over time.
choiceExplanations.3: Amazon Inspector is a vulnerability management service that scans workloads for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure. It does not analyze a role's activity or an instance's traffic history.

resources.title: Source data used in a Detective behavior graph

question:
A security team uses Amazon Detective and wants to study several related findings, together with the entities they involve, as one possible security event, to find the root cause of a multi-step attack.
Which Detective capability supports this?
choices: Detective finding groups
Detective's EKS audit logs data source
Detective's integration with Amazon Security Lake
Detective's entity profile for a single IP address
explanation: Detective finding groups let you examine multiple activities as they relate to a potential security event, because an attacker typically performs a sequence of actions that generate several findings. A finding group visualization shows the findings and entities involved in the event.

choiceExplanations.1: The EKS audit logs source package adds Kubernetes details, such as clusters and pods, to the behavior graph. It does not group related findings into one event.
choiceExplanations.2: The Security Lake integration lets Detective query and retrieve raw log data stored in Amazon Security Lake. It does not group findings.
choiceExplanations.3: An entity profile shows details and activity history for one entity. It does not combine several related findings into a single event.

question:
A media-streaming company runs 40 AWS accounts in one organization and has Amazon GuardDuty enabled in all of them. After a high-severity finding, the security team wants one place to trace the root cause across accounts, with up to a year of activity history and no new log collection or storage to manage. The solution must have the LEAST operational overhead.
Which solution should the team choose?
choices: Amazon GuardDuty in every account, with the team reviewing each account's findings in its own console
AWS Security Hub CSPM with cross-Region aggregation, with the team investigating the findings it aggregates
Amazon Athena queries over AWS CloudTrail logs and VPC flow logs that are delivered to a central Amazon S3 bucket
Amazon Detective, with a delegated administrator that enables every organization account in one behavior graph
explanation: Amazon Detective collects the CloudTrail, VPC flow log and GuardDuty data itself and keeps up to a year of it. The management account designates a Detective administrator, which can enable every organization account as a member of one organization behavior graph for cross-account root-cause analysis.

choiceExplanations.0: GuardDuty detects suspicious activity and produces the findings. It does not build the behavior graph and activity history that root-cause analysis needs, and reviewing account by account is not one place.
choiceExplanations.1: Security Hub CSPM gives a single view of aggregated findings and security-standard checks. It does not build activity visualizations from the underlying logs for root-cause analysis.
choiceExplanations.2: Athena can query logs in Amazon S3 with SQL, but the team would have to deliver and store the logs, create the tables and write the queries. That is new log storage and more operational work, with no prebuilt behavior graph.

question:
An application team runs microservices on Amazon EKS. Amazon Detective was enabled for the account in 2021, but while analysts investigate a GuardDuty Kubernetes finding, Detective shows no details about the Kubernetes pods, container images or Kubernetes subjects involved.
What should the team do?
choices: Turn on Detective's AWS security findings source package for the behavior graph
Turn on Detective's EKS audit logs source package for the behavior graph
Do nothing, because the Detective core package ingests EKS audit logs for every behavior graph
Start a Detective Investigation of the IAM role that the cluster nodes use
explanation: EKS audit logs is an optional Detective source package that adds in-depth information about EKS clusters, Kubernetes pods, container images and Kubernetes subjects. It is enabled by default only for behavior graphs created after July 26, 2022, so a graph from 2021 needs it enabled manually.

choiceExplanations.0: The AWS security findings package ingests findings that Security Hub CSPM aggregates. It does not add Kubernetes entity details to the graph.
choiceExplanations.2: The core package covers AWS CloudTrail logs, VPC flow logs and GuardDuty findings. EKS audit logs are optional and, for graphs created before July 26, 2022, must be enabled manually.
choiceExplanations.3: A Detective Investigation examines IAM users and roles for indicators of compromise. It does not ingest additional EKS data.

resources.title: Source data used in a Detective behavior graph

question:
A healthcare startup must give its auditors AWS's SOC and ISO compliance reports, and its legal team must also review and accept the HIPAA Business Associate Addendum with AWS before storing patient data.
Which single service provides both?
choices: AWS Config
AWS Artifact
AWS Control Tower
AWS Trusted Advisor
explanation: AWS Artifact provides on-demand downloads of AWS security and compliance documents, such as SOC, ISO and PCI reports. It also lets you review, accept and track agreements with AWS, such as a Business Associate Addendum.

choiceExplanations.0: AWS Config provides a detailed view of the configuration of your own AWS resources and how it changed over time. It does not provide AWS's compliance reports or agreements.
choiceExplanations.2: AWS Control Tower sets up and governs a multi-account environment with controls. It is not a source of AWS audit reports or agreements.
choiceExplanations.3: AWS Trusted Advisor inspects your environment and recommends ways to save money, improve availability and performance, or close security gaps. It does not offer AWS's audit reports or agreements.

question:
A hospital group has 25 accounts in an AWS Organizations organization with all features enabled. Its legal team wants the HIPAA Business Associate Addendum with AWS to cover every current and future account, accepted once.
Which action achieves this?
choices: Accept the agreement separately in each member account, on the Account agreements tab of AWS Artifact
Accept the agreement from a member account, on the Organization agreements tab of AWS Artifact
Download the agreement from the Reports page of AWS Artifact and have each account owner sign it
Accept the agreement from the management account, on the Organization agreements tab of AWS Artifact
explanation: With AWS Organizations, the owner of the management account can accept an agreement such as a BAA in AWS Artifact on behalf of all accounts. All existing and subsequent member accounts are automatically covered.

choiceExplanations.0: This works one account at a time, so it is not a single acceptance, and accounts added later would each need their own acceptance.
choiceExplanations.1: Organization agreements are accepted from the management account. Users of member accounts can only view and download the agreements accepted on their behalf.
choiceExplanations.2: A Business Associate Addendum is an agreement that you accept in AWS Artifact, not a report to download and sign. The Reports page holds audit documents such as SOC and ISO reports.

resources.title: Accepting agreements for your organization in AWS Artifact

question:
The CISO of a regional bank must show an auditor that the physical security of the data centers hosting the bank's AWS workloads is independently validated. The bank cannot visit AWS facilities, and the evidence must be downloadable on demand at no charge.
Which approach should the CISO take?
choices: Download AWS's third-party audit reports and certifications from AWS Artifact
Record the configuration of the bank's resources with AWS Config and give the auditor the history
Export the security checks that AWS Trusted Advisor runs against the bank's account
Generate a findings report for the bank's account with Amazon Inspector
explanation: AWS Artifact provides on-demand downloads of AWS audit reports and certifications from accreditation bodies that validate the implementation and operating effectiveness of AWS security controls, and you can submit them to auditors. AWS provides the documents and agreements free of charge.

choiceExplanations.1: AWS Config records the configuration of the bank's own resources. AWS's data centers are not resources in the account, and the history is not independent validation of them.
choiceExplanations.2: Trusted Advisor inspects the bank's own AWS environment and recommends improvements. It does not contain independent audit evidence about AWS facilities.
choiceExplanations.3: Amazon Inspector scans the bank's workloads for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure. It produces no evidence about AWS's data centers.

question:
A manufacturing company's vendor-risk team buys software through AWS Marketplace. It needs the independent security and compliance reports that those software vendors publish, and it must then pass one downloaded report to an external auditor.
What should the team do? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Download the vendors' reports from the Third-party reports tab in AWS Artifact
Download the vendors' reports from the AWS reports tab in AWS Artifact
Send the downloaded report to the auditor as an email attachment
Share the downloaded AWS Artifact report through a secure sharing service
Publish the downloaded report on the company intranet so the auditor can retrieve it
explanation: In AWS Artifact, the Third-party reports tab holds reports from independent software vendors that sell on AWS Marketplace. Each downloaded report is generated for you with a unique watermark, so it should be shared only through a secure sharing service, not by email or online.

choiceExplanations.1: The AWS reports tab holds AWS's own reports, such as SOC, PCI and C5. The vendors' reports are on the Third-party reports tab.
choiceExplanations.2: AWS says not to email Artifact reports as attachments. Each report is watermarked to you, so share it only through a secure sharing service.
choiceExplanations.4: AWS says not to share the reports online. Each report is watermarked to you, so share it only with people you trust, through a secure sharing service.

question:
A small startup wants one tool that checks its AWS account against AWS best practices and reports on cost optimization, security, fault tolerance and service limits. It does not want to install or configure anything.
Which service should it use?
choices: AWS Config
AWS CloudTrail
AWS Trusted Advisor
Amazon Inspector
explanation: AWS Trusted Advisor needs nothing installed. It inspects your AWS environment and recommends ways to save money, improve availability and performance, or close security gaps, in categories such as cost optimization, security, fault tolerance and service limits.

choiceExplanations.0: AWS Config provides a detailed view of how your resources are configured and how that changed over time. It is not an account-wide best-practice assessment that covers cost and service limits.
choiceExplanations.1: AWS CloudTrail records actions taken by users, roles and services as events for auditing. It does not assess the account against best practices.
choiceExplanations.3: Amazon Inspector is a vulnerability management service that scans workloads for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure. It does not report on cost, fault tolerance or service limits.

resources.title: Get started with Trusted Advisor Recommendations

question:
An operations team on an Enterprise Support plan wants a Lambda function to run automatically whenever an AWS Trusted Advisor check changes from no problems detected to action recommended.
Which Trusted Advisor capability supports this?
choices: Trusted Advisor organizational view reports for the organization
Trusted Advisor events sent to Amazon EventBridge
Trusted Advisor's Download all checks option in the console
Trusted Advisor's Refresh all checks option in the console
explanation: Trusted Advisor sends events to Amazon EventBridge when a check changes status. An EventBridge rule can then invoke targets such as an AWS Lambda function, which needs a qualifying paid Support plan.

choiceExplanations.0: Organizational view aggregates check results for all member accounts into reports. It does not invoke a target when a check changes status.
choiceExplanations.2: Download all checks creates an .xls file of the check results from the console. Nothing runs automatically.
choiceExplanations.3: Refresh all checks re-runs the checks on demand. It does not invoke a function when a status changes.

resources.title: Monitoring AWS Trusted Advisor check results with Amazon EventBridge

question:
A game studio runs 80 accounts in an AWS Organizations organization with all features enabled, and its management account is on Enterprise Support. Finance and security leads want one report that shows, for each member account, the results of best-practice checks across cost optimization, security, fault tolerance and service limits, with the LEAST effort.
What should the studio do?
choices: Use AWS Config with an organization aggregator to collect the results from every account
Use AWS Security Hub CSPM with a delegated administrator account to collect the findings from every account
Enable organizational view in AWS Trusted Advisor and create an organizational view report
Open AWS Trusted Advisor in each member account and merge the downloaded check results into one spreadsheet
explanation: Organizational view in AWS Trusted Advisor lets the management account see check results for all member accounts and create reports that aggregate them, including a summary and the affected resources for each account. It needs an organization with all features and a qualifying paid Support plan on the management account.

choiceExplanations.0: AWS Config shows how resources are configured and how that changed. It does not produce Trusted Advisor's cost optimization, fault tolerance and service limit check results.
choiceExplanations.1: Security Hub CSPM runs security-standard checks and collects security findings. It does not cover cost optimization, fault tolerance or service limits.
choiceExplanations.3: Downloading each account's results and merging them by hand works, but it is far more effort than the aggregated report that organizational view creates.

resources.title: Organizational view for AWS Trusted Advisor

question:
A company has just created an AWS account that is on the Basic Support plan. The team opens AWS Trusted Advisor.
Which TWO things can the team do? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Review the Trusted Advisor checks in the Cost optimization category
Review all of the Trusted Advisor checks in the Service limits category
Call the AWS Trusted Advisor API to read check results
Review selected Trusted Advisor checks in the Security category
Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that reacts to Trusted Advisor check status changes
explanation: With a Basic Support plan, Trusted Advisor gives access to all checks in the Service Limits category and selected checks in the Security and Fault tolerance categories. The full set of checks, the API and EventBridge rules for check results need a paid Support plan.

choiceExplanations.0: Basic Support covers only the Service Limits category and selected Security and Fault tolerance checks. Cost optimization checks need a paid plan.
choiceExplanations.2: Programmatic access to all Trusted Advisor checks through the API comes with a paid Support plan, not Basic Support.
choiceExplanations.4: Creating an EventBridge rule for Trusted Advisor checks requires a paid Support plan.

question:
A support engineer without an AWS account sign-in wants a public page that shows whether AWS currently reports a problem with a service in a Region, plus the service interruptions from the last 12 months.
Which should the engineer open?
choices: AWS Config
AWS CloudTrail
AWS Trusted Advisor
AWS Health Dashboard
explanation: The AWS Health Dashboard Service health page shows public events for AWS services across Regions without any sign-in. Its Service history table lists all AWS service interruptions for the last 12 months.

choiceExplanations.0: AWS Config shows the configuration of resources in your own account, so it needs an account and says nothing about AWS service outages.
choiceExplanations.1: AWS CloudTrail records actions taken in your own account. It does not report AWS service issues.
choiceExplanations.2: AWS Trusted Advisor inspects your own AWS environment for recommendations and needs an account. It does not list AWS service interruptions.

question:
A platform team wants to plan around upcoming AWS maintenance that affects its own resources, and to see those scheduled changes on a monthly calendar.
Which part of the AWS Health Dashboard should the team use?
choices: AWS Health Dashboard, Your account health: Scheduled changes
AWS Health Dashboard, Service health: Service history
AWS Health Dashboard, Your account health: Event log
AWS Health Dashboard, Your account health: Other notifications
explanation: The Scheduled changes tab under Your account health shows upcoming events that might affect your account, such as scheduled maintenance, and offers a calendar view that maps them onto a monthly calendar.

choiceExplanations.1: Service history is part of the public Service health page and lists past service interruptions from the last 12 months. It is not specific to your resources and is not about upcoming changes.
choiceExplanations.2: The Event log lists AWS Health events from the past 90 days in a filterable table. The calendar view is on the Scheduled changes tab.
choiceExplanations.3: Other notifications shows other notifications and ongoing events from the past seven days, such as certificate rotations and billing notifications, not a calendar of scheduled changes.

resources.title: Viewing your account events in the AWS Health Dashboard

question:
An AWS Organizations organization has all features enabled and 60 member accounts. The site-reliability team works in its own member account and must see AWS Health events for every member account in one place, while the management account stays restricted.
Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Sign in to each member account every morning and review its Your account health page in the AWS Health Dashboard
Bookmark the AWS Health Dashboard Service health page, which lists the events of all member accounts
Enable organizational view in the AWS Health Dashboard by signing in to the management account
Use the AWS Trusted Advisor organizational view to read the AWS Health events of the member accounts
Register the site-reliability team's member account as a delegated administrator for AWS Health organizational view
explanation: Organizational view, enabled from the management account of an organization with all features, gives one view of AWS Health events across the organization. Registering a delegated administrator lets a member account see that view, which keeps the management account restricted.

choiceExplanations.0: Each account's page shows only that account's events, so this is 60 separate places rather than one.
choiceExplanations.1: The Service health page shows public events that are not specific to any account. It does not list the events of member accounts.
choiceExplanations.3: Trusted Advisor organizational view aggregates Trusted Advisor check results, not AWS Health events.

resources.title: Aggregating AWS Health events across accounts
Managing delegated administrator views for an organization

question:
An e-commerce startup is on the Basic Support plan. It wants a ticket created automatically in its tracker whenever AWS announces that one of its EC2 instances is scheduled for retirement.
Which approach works?
choices: Poll the AWS Health API every few minutes from a scheduled AWS Lambda function that opens the ticket
Create an Amazon EventBridge rule for AWS Health Dashboard events, with a Lambda function target that opens the ticket
Upgrade to a paid support plan first, because the AWS Health Dashboard sends events to EventBridge only for paid plans
Scrape the AWS Health Dashboard RSS feed from a scheduled Lambda function that opens the ticket
explanation: All AWS customers can receive AWS Health events through Amazon EventBridge at no additional cost, and rules can invoke targets such as a Lambda function. That is the recommended way to ingest events programmatically.

choiceExplanations.0: The AWS Health API needs a qualifying paid Support plan, so it is not available on Basic Support.
choiceExplanations.2: A paid plan is not needed. All customers can receive AWS Health events through EventBridge at no additional cost.
choiceExplanations.3: AWS says the RSS feed format can change and that scraping it might not provide all relevant data. It recommends integrating with EventBridge to ingest health events programmatically.

resources.title: Monitoring events in AWS Health with Amazon EventBridge

question:
A cloud team wants developers to browse a catalog of pre-approved architectures and launch them in one step. The team wants a role that it controls to create the resources, so developers need no direct permissions for the services inside each architecture.
Which service should it use?
choices: AWS Config
AWS Service Catalog
AWS Control Tower
AWS CloudFormation
explanation: AWS Service Catalog lets administrators assemble portfolios of approved products that users browse and launch themselves. A launch constraint names the IAM role that Service Catalog assumes when launching, so end users need only minimal permissions.

choiceExplanations.0: AWS Config shows how resources are configured and how that changed. It does not offer products for users to launch.
choiceExplanations.2: AWS Control Tower sets up and governs a multi-account environment with controls. It is not a catalog of approved products that developers launch.
choiceExplanations.3: AWS CloudFormation provisions resources from templates. By itself it has no portfolios of approved products with launch roles for end users.

question:
An administrator offers a Service Catalog product whose CloudFormation template lets users choose any EC2 instance type. Interns must be able to launch the product with only small instance types.
Which Service Catalog feature should the administrator apply to the product in the portfolio?
choices: Service Catalog launch constraints
Service Catalog notification constraints
Service Catalog template constraints
Service Catalog tag update constraints
explanation: A template constraint narrows the allowed values for the parameters in the product's CloudFormation template, for example limiting the instance types that end users can choose. It is applied to a product in a portfolio.

choiceExplanations.0: A launch constraint specifies the IAM role that Service Catalog assumes when users launch, update or terminate a product. It does not restrict the parameter values users can pick.
choiceExplanations.1: A notification constraint specifies an Amazon SNS topic that receives notifications about stack events. It does not limit parameter values.
choiceExplanations.3: A tag update constraint allows or disallows users to update tags on the resources of a provisioned product. It does not limit parameter values.

question:
A university's central cloud team maintains approved CloudFormation-based products for 50 departmental accounts in its organization. Any change the team makes to a product or its constraints must reach every account without redeploying anything, and department administrators must not be able to alter the products or constraints.
Which solution meets these requirements?
choices: Share the AWS Service Catalog portfolio through AWS Organizations and let each department import it
Deploy a copy of the AWS Service Catalog portfolio into every account with AWS CloudFormation StackSets
Publish the templates in a shared Amazon S3 bucket and give every account read access to it
Attach service control policies that allow only the approved instance types and Regions
explanation: Sharing a portfolio through AWS Organizations lets recipient administrators import it. The imported portfolio is not a copy: changes to products and constraints propagate to it, and the recipient administrator cannot change them.

choiceExplanations.1: Deploying a copy with StackSets puts an independent catalog in each account, so every update must be redeployed to propagate. A shared reference stays in sync automatically.
choiceExplanations.2: A bucket of templates gives accounts files to deploy, but no catalog of approved products, no constraints and nothing that stays in sync with the products.
choiceExplanations.3: Service control policies set limits on the actions that users and roles can perform. They do not provide products to launch or propagate product changes.

question:
A central team shares an AWS Service Catalog portfolio with other accounts. Its products carry a launch constraint that names a role in the central account. As the administrator of a recipient account, you want products launched in your account to use a launch role from your own account instead.
What should you do?
choices: Edit the launch constraint on the imported portfolio in AWS Service Catalog
Remove the launch constraint from the imported portfolio in AWS Service Catalog, so users launch with their own credentials
Re-share the imported portfolio from your account in AWS Service Catalog with a new launch constraint
Add the product to a local portfolio in AWS Service Catalog and apply a different launch constraint to it
explanation: A recipient administrator cannot change the products or constraints of an imported portfolio. To override a launch constraint, the administrator adds the product to a local portfolio in the recipient account and applies a different launch constraint there.

choiceExplanations.0: The recipient administrator cannot change the products or constraints of an imported portfolio.
choiceExplanations.1: The recipient administrator cannot change the constraints of an imported portfolio, and launching with users' own credentials would not use the required launch role.
choiceExplanations.2: You cannot re-share products from a portfolio that has been imported or shared.

question:
A company runs workloads on Amazon EC2 under its own operating system licenses. The agreement with the OS vendor expires next month and will not be renewed, but the workloads must keep running with compliant licenses and without being redeployed.
Which service lets the company switch to AWS-provided licenses?
choices: AWS Config
AWS Control Tower
AWS License Manager
AWS Systems Manager
explanation: AWS License Manager can change a license type between AWS-provided licensing and Bring Your Own License (BYOL) without redeploying existing workloads. Switching from BYOL to AWS-provided licenses keeps workloads running when a license agreement is about to expire.

choiceExplanations.0: AWS Config records resource configuration and its changes. It does not change how instances are licensed.
choiceExplanations.1: AWS Control Tower sets up and governs a multi-account environment. It does not convert license types.
choiceExplanations.3: Systems Manager Inventory collects metadata, such as installed applications, from managed nodes. It does not switch instances between BYOL and AWS-provided licenses.

resources.title: License type conversions in License Manager

question:
A company counts the vCPUs of a licensed product with AWS License Manager. It wants EC2 launches that would exceed the number of licenses it owns to be blocked, not just reported.
Which License Manager configuration should it use?
choices: A License Manager self-managed license with a hard limit
A License Manager self-managed license with a soft limit
License Manager inventory search over Systems Manager inventory
License Manager license type conversion to AWS-provided licenses
explanation: A self-managed license specifies the licensing terms and a usage limit. When the limit is exceeded, a soft limit notifies you, while a hard limit prevents the resource from deploying.

choiceExplanations.1: A soft limit only notifies you when the license limit is exceeded. It does not stop the launch.
choiceExplanations.2: Inventory search discovers on-premises applications through Systems Manager inventory so that rules can be attached and usage tracked. It is not a limit setting.
choiceExplanations.3: License type conversion switches instances between AWS-provided licenses and BYOL. It does not block launches.

resources.title: Create a self-managed license in License Manager

question:
A government agency runs licensed software across 30 accounts and several Regions of one AWS organization. The vendor licenses by socket. Auditors want one central count of license use, launches beyond the purchased count must be blocked, and the agency's on-premises servers running the same software must appear on the same dashboard.
Which solution meets these requirements?
choices: AWS Systems Manager Inventory with a Resource Data Sync to a central Amazon S3 bucket, queried with Amazon Athena
AWS Config recording in every account, with the license counts reviewed from the configuration history after launches
AWS Organizations service control policies that cap how many instances each account can launch
AWS License Manager self-managed licenses with hard limits, shared across the organization, and inventory search
explanation: License Manager lets you centrally track licenses and enforce limits across Regions and accounts in an organization, and a hard limit prevents a resource from deploying. Its inventory search discovers on-premises applications through Systems Manager inventory so they appear in the same dashboard.

choiceExplanations.0: Inventory collects metadata from managed nodes and can be queried, but it holds no license limits and cannot block a launch.
choiceExplanations.1: AWS Config records resource configuration and its history. It holds no license rules and does not stop a launch that would exceed the purchased count.
choiceExplanations.2: Service control policies set limits on the actions that users and roles can perform. They do not count license usage or cap instances against a purchased license count.

question:
An independent software vendor licenses its product per physical socket and requires each license to stay on the same physical host for at least 90 days. A company runs the product on Amazon EC2 Dedicated Hosts and wants AWS License Manager to enforce these terms.
Which self-managed license configuration meets the requirements?
choices: A License Manager self-managed license that counts vCPUs, with a 90-day license affinity to host and Dedicated Host tenancy
A License Manager self-managed license that counts sockets, with 90-day license affinity and Dedicated Host tenancy
A License Manager self-managed license that counts instances, with a Dedicated Instance tenancy rule and a maximum vCPUs rule
A License Manager self-managed license that counts sockets, with Shared tenancy and a minimum sockets rule
explanation: The license affinity to host rule restricts license use to a host for a set number of days, and it needs a counting type of Cores or Sockets. When the counting type is Sockets, the tenancy rule must be Dedicated Hosts.

choiceExplanations.0: The license affinity to host rule is available only when the counting type is Cores or Sockets, so a vCPU-counted license cannot enforce it, and vCPUs do not match a per-socket license.
choiceExplanations.2: Counting instances does not match a per-socket license and does not offer the license affinity to host rule. Dedicated Instance tenancy is also not Dedicated Hosts.
choiceExplanations.3: Dedicated Hosts are required when the counting type is Cores or Sockets, so Shared tenancy is not a valid choice for a socket-counted license. This option also has no license affinity rule.

resources.title: Self-managed license parameters and rules in License Manager

question:
A logistics company wants its architects to answer a structured set of best-practice questions about each workload, see the high and medium risk issues that result with an improvement plan, and share the review with other AWS accounts.
Which AWS tool should it use?
choices: AWS Trusted Advisor
AWS Well-Architected Tool
AWS Config
AWS Control Tower
explanation: In the AWS Well-Architected Tool you define a workload, answer lens questions and get high and medium risk issues with an improvement plan. You can also share the workload with other accounts, users, organizations or OUs in the same Region.

choiceExplanations.0: AWS Trusted Advisor inspects your AWS environment automatically and recommends improvements. It is not a questionnaire that architects answer, and it has no shared workload reviews.
choiceExplanations.2: AWS Config provides a view of how your resources are configured over time. It does not run a question-based review or produce an improvement plan.
choiceExplanations.3: AWS Control Tower sets up and governs a multi-account environment with controls. It is not a workload review tool.

resources.title: Share a workload in AWS Well-Architected Tool

question:
An architecture team has answered all the questions for a workload in the AWS Well-Architected Tool. It wants to save the workload's current state as a fixed snapshot inside the tool, so it can measure progress after the issues are fixed.
Which feature should it use?
choices: A Well-Architected Tool custom lens
A Well-Architected Tool profile
A Well-Architected Tool workload report
A Well-Architected Tool milestone
explanation: A milestone records the state of a workload at a point in time. You save one after completing the questions and more as you improve the workload, to measure progress. After a milestone is saved, its workload data cannot be changed.

choiceExplanations.0: A custom lens holds your own pillars, questions, best practices and improvement plan. It does not record the workload's state.
choiceExplanations.1: A profile holds business-context questions and answers that prioritize the review questions and risks. It does not record the workload's state.
choiceExplanations.2: A workload report shows the current responses, notes and risk counts, and can be shared with people who have no tool access. A saved milestone is what records the state to measure progress.

resources.title: Saving a milestone for a workload in AWS WA Tool

question:
A SaaS company wants to review its multi-tenant platform against AWS best practices written for SaaS workloads, and also add its own internal engineering-standard questions to the same review. Managers without console access need a document with the results.
Which solution meets these requirements?
choices: AWS Trusted Advisor, with the check results downloaded for the managers
AWS Config, with custom rules for the internal engineering standards
AWS Well-Architected Tool, applying the SaaS lens and a custom lens, then generating a report
AWS Service Catalog, with a portfolio of products that enforce the internal engineering standards
explanation: The Lens Catalog in the AWS Well-Architected Tool includes an official SaaS lens, and custom lenses let a company add its own questions and best practices to a review. A workload report lets people without access to the tool see the responses, notes and risks.

choiceExplanations.0: Trusted Advisor runs automated checks against the account. It has no SaaS lens and no way to add the company's own review questions.
choiceExplanations.1: AWS Config evaluates the configuration of resources. It offers no question-based review and no SaaS best-practice guidance.
choiceExplanations.3: Service Catalog offers approved products for users to launch. It does not review a workload against best practices.

resources.title: Lens Catalog for AWS WA Tool
Custom lenses for workloads in AWS WA Tool
Generate a workload report in AWS Well-Architected Tool

question:
Architects at a payments firm find that the default AWS Well-Architected Tool review asks many questions that matter little to their business. They want the tool to focus on the questions and risks most relevant to their business goals, without writing new questions or adding lenses.
What should they do?
choices: Attach a Well-Architected Tool profile with the firm's business context to the workload
Create a Well-Architected Tool custom lens that contains a smaller set of review questions
Save a Well-Architected Tool milestone before the questions are answered
Apply an industry lens from the Well-Architected Tool Lens Catalog to the workload
explanation: A profile holds business context and goals. The Well-Architected Tool uses it to prioritize the review questions that are relevant to the business, and to show which risks to address first in the improvement plan.

choiceExplanations.1: A custom lens means writing new questions and best practices, which the architects want to avoid, and it adds a lens.
choiceExplanations.2: A milestone records the state of a workload at a point in time. It does not change which questions or risks are prioritized.
choiceExplanations.3: A Lens Catalog lens adds another set of AWS questions and best practices to the review. It adds lenses and does not prioritize questions by the firm's business context.

question:
A data team runs a nightly pipeline: an AWS Glue job, then an Amazon Athena query that may start only after the job finishes. Each step must wait for the one before it, and failed steps must be retried, without the team writing polling code.
Which AWS service should the team use?
choices: AWS Lambda functions
AWS Step Functions
Amazon SNS topics
Amazon SQS queues
explanation: AWS Step Functions can start a Glue job or an Athena query and, with the Run a Job (.sync) integration pattern, wait for it to finish before moving to the next state. Retry settings on each state handle failed steps, so no polling code is needed.

choiceExplanations.0: AWS Lambda runs code but does not orchestrate a sequence of long-running jobs; waiting for a job to finish would mean writing polling logic inside the functions.
choiceExplanations.2: Amazon SNS publishes notifications to subscribers. It does not run an ordered sequence of steps or wait for a job to finish.
choiceExplanations.3: Amazon SQS queues messages between components. It does not track a multi-step workflow or wait for a Glue job or an Athena query to finish.

resources.title: Discover service integration patterns in Step Functions
Start an AWS Glue job with Step Functions

question:
An order workflow in AWS Step Functions receives a list of order lines, and the number of lines is different for every order. Every line must go through the same validation steps at the same time instead of one after another.
Which Step Functions state should the workflow use?
choices: A Step Functions Wait state
A Step Functions Choice state
A Step Functions Parallel state
A Step Functions Map state
explanation: A Map state runs the same set of steps for each item in a dataset, and its iterations run in parallel. That fits a list whose length changes with every order.

choiceExplanations.0: A Wait state only delays the workflow for a set time or until a timestamp. It does not process the items of a list.
choiceExplanations.1: A Choice state adds conditional logic and moves to one next state. It does not repeat steps for each item.
choiceExplanations.2: A Parallel state runs the branches that are written into the state machine definition, so the number of branches does not follow the length of the list.

question:
An expense-approval process validates a claim with AWS Lambda, emails a manager, and then must pause for up to three days until the manager answers before paying out. No servers may run while it waits, auditors need the history of every run, and the team wants the LEAST custom code.
Which solution should the team build?
choices: An AWS Step Functions Standard workflow that pauses at a task by using the callback (task token) pattern
An AWS Step Functions Express workflow that pauses at a task by using the callback (task token) pattern
An Amazon SQS queue with a Lambda function that stays running until the manager replies
An Amazon EventBridge schedule that invokes a Lambda function every few minutes to look for a reply
explanation: A Standard workflow can run for up to a year, and the callback pattern pauses a task until a task token is returned, which suits waiting for a human approval. Standard workflows also keep an execution history that can be retrieved after the run.

choiceExplanations.1: Express workflows run for at most five minutes and do not support the callback (.waitForTaskToken) pattern, so they cannot wait three days for an answer.
choiceExplanations.2: An SQS queue only holds messages. A function that stays running until the manager replies keeps compute running while it waits, and nothing tracks the state or history of each claim.
choiceExplanations.3: A scheduled poll needs custom code to look up and store each claim's state and gives no built-in history of each run, which is more custom code than a workflow needs.

resources.title: Discover service integration patterns in Step Functions
Choosing workflow type in Step Functions

question:
A media startup keeps a CSV file with four million rows in Amazon S3. A Step Functions workflow must run a Lambda function for every row, with thousands of iterations in parallel, and the execution history would exceed 25,000 events.
Which Step Functions feature should the startup use?
choices: A Step Functions Parallel state that defines one branch for each row
A Step Functions Map state in Inline mode that reads the rows from the state input
A Step Functions Map state in Distributed mode that reads the CSV file directly from Amazon S3
A Step Functions Choice state that loops back to the Lambda task until all rows are done
